title: How Lonely Lies the City
subtitle: Lamentations 1
description: The widowed city sits empty, stretches out her hands, and finds no one to comfort her.
paragraphs: The fall has already happened when this book opens. There is no battle in it, no siege engine, no report. There is a city sitting empty, and the first poem of the five does not tell her story so much as sit down beside her and look. “How lonely lies the city, once so full of people! She who was great among the nations has become a widow. The princess of the provinces has become a slave.” Verse 2 stays with her through the night: “She weeps aloud in the night, with tears upon her cheeks. Among all her lovers there is no one to comfort her.” The lovers are the allies she trusted instead of God, Egypt and the nations, and every one of them is gone. Four times in this poem the same fact comes back in different words, and the poem means for it to be counted: there is no one to comfort her.

What is left is a land emptied out. “Judah has gone into exile under affliction and harsh slavery; she dwells among the nations but finds no place to rest.” The roads themselves are in mourning in verse 4, “because no one comes to her appointed feasts,” and her gates stand deserted while her priests groan. Her princes, the poem says in verse 6, “are like deer that find no pasture,” too weak to run from the hunter. And the poem does not hide why. Verse 5 gives the reason in plain words: “For the LORD has brought her grief because of her many transgressions. Her children have gone away as captives before the enemy.” This is grief with the confession already inside it. The city is not presented as an innocent victim of a stronger empire. She is a widow who knows whose hand allowed the house to empty.

Halfway through, the poem stops describing her and lets her speak, and her first words are a plea to be seen. Her treasures are gone, traded away for bread: “They have traded their treasures for food to keep themselves alive.” She has watched the nations walk into the sanctuary they were forbidden to enter, and she says in verse 11, “Look, O LORD, and consider, for I have become despised.” Then in verse 12 she turns from heaven to the road, to anyone passing by a ruin on the way to somewhere else: “Is this nothing to you, all you who pass by? Look around and see! Is there any sorrow like mine, which was inflicted on me, which the LORD made me suffer on the day of His fierce anger?” It is the poem's sharpest question, and it is aimed at everyone who would rather not slow down.

Her description of what God has done to her is unsparing. “He made me desolate, faint all the day long.” Her transgressions, she says in verse 14, were bound into a yoke by His hand and draped over her neck until her strength broke. Her mighty men were rejected, her young warriors crushed like grapes in a winepress. Verse 16 returns to the tears: “For these things I weep; my eyes flow with tears. For there is no one nearby to comfort me, no one to revive my soul.” And verse 17 gives the picture the whole poem has been building toward: “Zion stretches out her hands, but there is no one to comfort her.” Hands out, and nobody there. The poem holds that picture without rushing past it.

The last movement is hers too, and it is where the confession comes out whole. “The LORD is righteous, yet I rebelled against His command. Listen, all you people; look upon my suffering. My young men and maidens have gone into captivity.” She does not ask God to admit He was wrong. She says He was right, and she rebelled, and both of those are true in the same breath. Her distress is described from the inside in verse 20: “Outside, the sword bereaves; inside, there is death.” Her enemies, she notes, have heard of her trouble and are glad of it, “glad that You have caused it,” and her final request is not comfort but justice, that the day God announced would reach them too. The poem closes with her own summary of herself: “For my groans are many, and my heart is faint.” No rescue arrives. The first poem ends with the widow still sitting in the ashes, and the book lets her sit there while the second poem picks up the harder question: not who left her, but who struck her.

title: The Lord Is Like an Enemy
subtitle: Lamentations 2
description: The second poem names the attacker, and it is not Babylon: the LORD has bent His bow against His own city.
paragraphs: The second poem is harder than the first, because it names the attacker. Babylon dug the trenches, but this poem barely looks at Babylon. It looks up. “How the Lord has covered the Daughter of Zion with the cloud of His anger! He has cast the glory of Israel from heaven to earth. He has abandoned His footstool in the day of His anger.” The footstool is the temple, God's own house, and the poem says God abandoned it. Verse 2 refuses any softening: “Without pity the Lord has swallowed up all the dwellings of Jacob.” Verse 3 has Him burning through His own people, “like a flaming fire that consumes everything around it.” The poem is not questioning God's right. It is recording, with something like shock, how completely He used it.

The shock deepens in verses 4 through 8, because the enemy in this poem carries God's own bow. “Like a foe He has killed all who were pleasing to the eye.” Verse 5 says it flatly, the line this episode is named for: “The Lord is like an enemy; He has swallowed up Israel.” He destroyed His own meeting place: “The LORD has made Zion forget her appointed feasts and Sabbaths,” and verse 7, “The Lord has rejected His altar; He has abandoned His sanctuary.” The feasts, the altar, the Sabbaths, the king, the priest, all swept in one list, as if God had decided to unbuild His own house piece by piece. And the destruction was not a rage out of control. Verse 8 pictures it as measured work: “He stretched out a measuring line and did not withdraw His hand from destroying.” A builder's line, used in reverse.

Then the poem goes quiet. Verse 9 ends the inventory with the worst item last: “Her king and her princes are exiled among the nations, the law is no more, and even her prophets find no vision from the LORD.” The word of God itself has gone silent. The elders sit on the ground saying nothing, dust on their heads. At verse 11 the watcher watching all this breaks down himself: “My eyes fail from weeping; I am churning within. My heart is poured out in grief over the destruction of the daughter of my people, because children and infants faint in the streets of the city.” The children are the poem's center of gravity. They cry to their mothers in verse 12, “Where is the grain and wine?”, fading in their arms in the street. And the watcher asks the question nobody in the book can answer: “For your wound is as deep as the sea. Who can ever heal you?”

Part of the blame lands where the first poem did not put it: on the prophets who lied. “The visions of your prophets were empty and deceptive; they did not expose your guilt to ward off your captivity.” For years the city had been told peace was coming, and the men who told her that are named here as one of the causes of the ruin. Meanwhile the passersby from the first poem are back, and now they are mocking: “Is this the city that was called the perfection of beauty, the joy of all the earth?” The enemies say outright, “We have swallowed her up. This is the day for which we have waited.” But verse 17 pulls the credit away from them and hands it back to heaven: “The LORD has done what He planned; He has accomplished His decree, which He ordained in days of old.” What Jeremiah announced for forty years, what the covenant warnings had said for centuries, had simply come due.

The poem ends not with an answer but with an instruction and a prayer. The instruction, verse 19, is the only thing the book tells anyone to do: “Arise, cry out in the night from the first watch of the night. Pour out your heart like water in the presence of the Lord. Lift up your hands to Him for the lives of your children who are fainting from hunger on the corner of every street.” Then the poem itself does it, and the prayer is horrifying on purpose. “Look, O LORD, and consider: Whom have You ever treated like this? Should women eat their offspring, the infants they have nurtured? Should priests and prophets be killed in the sanctuary of the Lord?” Young and old lie together in the dust, and verse 21 says, “You have slain them in the day of Your anger; You have slaughtered them without compassion.” The last line offers no relief: “In the day of the LORD’s anger no one escaped or survived.” The poem lays the whole atrocity at God's feet, not to accuse Him of evil, but because there is no one else left to appeal to. If the Lord was the enemy, the Lord is also the only court still in session.

title: Great Is Your Faithfulness
subtitle: Lamentations 3
description: One unnamed sufferer tells what affliction felt like from inside, and finds hope by an act of memory.
paragraphs: The third poem narrows to one voice, and it is the most personal speaking in the book. “I am the man who has seen affliction under the rod of God’s wrath.” He never names himself. He speaks as one sufferer standing for all of them, and for the first eighteen verses there is no city, no nation, only a single man and what God has done to him. “He has driven me away and made me walk in darkness instead of light.” Verse 5 stacks the images: “He has besieged me and surrounded me with bitterness and hardship.” Verse 7 closes every exit: “He has walled me in so I cannot escape; He has weighed me down with chains.” And verse 8 lands on the worst of it. It is not the pain. It is the silence above it: “Even when I cry out and plead for help, He shuts out my prayer.”

The images keep coming, and they get wilder. In verse 10 God is not a king or a judge but an animal waiting in cover: “He is a bear lying in wait, a lion hiding in ambush.” In verses 12 and 13 the sufferer is not the prey but the target: “He bent His bow and set me as the target for His arrow. He pierced my kidneys with His arrows.” His own people mock him in song all day. Verse 15 says, “He has filled me with bitterness; He has intoxicated me with wormwood,” and verse 16 describes humiliation at ground level: “He has ground my teeth with gravel and trampled me in the dust.” By verse 17 he has lost even the memory of better days: “My soul has been deprived of peace; I have forgotten what prosperity is.” And verse 18 is the bottom of the pit, stated as a conclusion he has reasoned his way to: “My strength has perished, along with my hope from the LORD.”

Then, at verse 19, he does something deliberate. He orders his own memory. “Remember my affliction and wandering, the wormwood and the gall.” He does not tell himself to forget the worst. He tells himself to remember it, all of it, and his soul, he says, “remembers and is humbled within me.” And out of that act of remembering, not out of any change in his circumstances, comes verse 21: “Yet I call this to mind, and therefore I have hope.” Nothing around him has improved. The walls are still up, the prayer still unanswered, the city still down. What changes is what he calls to mind next, and it is the most famous passage in the book: “Because of the loving devotion of the LORD we are not consumed, for His mercies never fail. They are new every morning; great is Your faithfulness!” Notice where it stands. It is not the city's anthem after a rescue. It is one ruined man, mid affliction, deciding what is still true.

Verse 24 shows the decision becoming a possession. His soul says, “The LORD is my portion,” and draws the conclusion: “therefore I will hope in Him.” A portion is an inheritance, the share of the land a family lives on. His land is ash, so he takes God Himself as the share. From there the poem's voice steadies into instruction, a man teaching himself out loud. “The LORD is good to those who wait for Him, to the soul who seeks Him. It is good to wait quietly for the salvation of the LORD. It is good for a man to bear the yoke while he is still young.” Verse 28 gives the posture: “Let him sit alone in silence, for the LORD has laid it upon him.” Verse 29 gives even the dust a hope attached to it: “Let him bury his face in the dust,” then, as a separate small sentence, “perhaps there is still hope.” Verse 30 goes furthest: “Let him offer his cheek to the one who would strike him; let him be filled with reproach.”

The first half of the poem ends by giving the reason all of this is bearable, and the reason is God's character, not the sufferer's strength. “For the Lord will not cast us off forever.” Verse 32 holds grief and compassion in one sentence: “Even if He causes grief, He will show compassion according to His abundant loving devotion.” And verse 33 reaches the deepest claim in the poem: “For He does not willingly afflict or grieve the sons of men.” The affliction is real, it came from God's hand, and yet it is not where God's heart is. The man's hope is not that he misread his pain. It is that the God who sent it does not delight in it, and will not leave him in it forever. The poem does not stop here, though. The same voice turns, in the second half, from his own wounds to everyone's ways, and from endurance to examination.

title: Let Us Examine Our Ways
subtitle: Lamentations 3
description: The same voice turns from endurance to examination: confession, the pit, and a God who draws near.
paragraphs: The second half of the third poem opens by finishing a thought: there are things God does not do, and the poem lists them before it says anything else. To crush prisoners underfoot, to deny a man justice before the Most High, to subvert a man in his lawsuit, and then the verdict, arriving as the tail of the list: “of these the Lord does not approve.” Injustice happens in the world, and this sufferer, who has suffered plenty of it, refuses to lay it at God's charge as though God enjoyed it. Verse 37 asks who really governs outcomes: “Who has spoken and it came to pass, unless the Lord has ordained it?” Verse 38 holds both sides in one question: “Do not both adversity and good come from the mouth of the Most High?” And verse 39 turns the whole doctrine on the hearer: “Why should any mortal man complain, in view of his sins?” If God is sovereign and man is guilty, complaint is the wrong posture. Something else is required.

Verse 40 names it, and it is the poem's great turning verb. “Let us examine and test our ways, and turn back to the LORD.” Not examine Babylon's ways, not examine the prophets who lied, but our ways. Verse 41 lifts the examination into prayer: “Let us lift up our hearts and hands to God in heaven.” Then verse 42 makes the confession the first half of the book has been circling: “We have sinned and rebelled; You have not forgiven.” Four words of confession, three of consequence, no defense in between. What follows in verses 43 to 45 is the consequence described without flinching: “You have covered Yourself in anger and pursued us; You have killed without pity.” Verse 44 gives the reason heaven felt shut in the poem's first half: “You have covered Yourself with a cloud that no prayer can pass through.” Verse 45 gives the world's verdict on them: “You have made us scum and refuse among the nations.” The confession does not produce immediate relief. It produces honesty, and the honesty is the relief's beginning.

The grief does not lift just because the confession is honest. The enemies are still standing there with their mouths open in verse 46: “All our enemies open their mouths against us.” Verse 47 pairs the trap and the fall: “Panic and pitfall have come upon us,” and then, as its own fragment, “devastation and destruction.” The sufferer's tears in verse 48 are no longer only for himself: “Streams of tears flow from my eyes over the destruction of the daughter of my people.” Verse 49 sets the terms of his weeping: “My eyes overflow unceasingly, without relief,” and verse 50 the condition that ends it, “until the LORD looks down from heaven and sees.” He will cry until heaven looks. Verse 51 explains why he cannot stop: “My eyes bring grief to my soul because of all the daughters of my city.” Seeing is itself the wound now.

Then the poem drops back into the man's own story, and it drops literally. Verse 52: “Without cause my enemies hunted me like a bird.” Verse 53: “They dropped me alive into a pit and cast stones upon me.” Verse 54 reaches the drowning line: “The waters flowed over my head, and I thought I was going to die.” Whether the pit is literal or the whole siege felt from inside, the poem tells it as one man's memory of going under. And from the bottom of it he prayed. Verse 55: “I called on Your name, O LORD, out of the depths of the Pit.” Verse 56 records that the prayer the first half said was shut out was, in fact, heard; his plea had been, “Do not ignore my cry for relief.” Verse 57 is the answer, and it is short enough to carry for a lifetime: “You drew near when I called on You; You said,” and then God's own three words, “Do not be afraid.” Verse 58 draws the conclusion: “You defend my cause, O Lord; You redeem my life.”

The poem closes by handing the enemies over. Verse 59 asks for a verdict, not revenge of his own taking: “You have seen, O LORD, the wrong done to me; vindicate my cause!” He recites what God has already witnessed, the insults and the plots: “O LORD, You have heard their insults, all their plots against me.” Verse 63 has the mockers' whole day reduced to a soundtrack: “When they sit and when they rise, see how they mock me in song.” Then verses 64 to 66 ask God to return their own work on their own heads: “You will pay them back what they deserve, O LORD, according to the work of their hands.” The final verse of the poem is a curse requested, not performed: “You will pursue them in anger and exterminate them from under Your heavens, O LORD.” The man who began the poem walled in and silenced ends it speaking freely, confessing honestly, weeping openly, and leaving vengeance where he has left everything else by now: in the hands of the God whose faithfulness he swore by in the dark.

title: The Gold Has Become Tarnished
subtitle: Lamentations 4
description: The fourth poem holds what the city was up against what it is, and finds her punishment has a limit.
paragraphs: The fourth poem is built on two words: how, and once. It walks through the city holding what people used to be up against what they are now, and the contrast is the whole poem. It opens with the metal of the sanctuary itself: “How the gold has become tarnished, the pure gold has become dull!” The temple's gems lie scattered on street corners. Then the gold becomes people. “How the precious sons of Zion, once worth their weight in pure gold, are now esteemed as jars of clay, the work of a potter’s hands!” Verse 3 makes the comparison at the level of animals: “Even jackals offer their breasts to nurse their young, but the daughter of my people has become cruel, like an ostrich in the wilderness.” The siege has not only starved the city. It has inverted nature in her. Verse 4: “Little children beg for bread, but no one gives them any.” Verse 5: “Those who once ate delicacies are destitute in the streets,” and those raised in crimson now huddle in ash heaps.

The reversals get worse as faces come into view. Verse 6 reaches for the most infamous comparison available and says the fall of Jerusalem outdid it: “The punishment of the daughter of my people is greater than that of Sodom, which was overthrown in an instant.” Sodom at least ended quickly; this city starved slowly. Verse 7 remembers the dignitaries as they were, “brighter than snow, whiter than milk,” bodies “more ruddy than rubies,” and verse 8 shows them now: “But now their appearance is blacker than soot; they are not recognized in the streets. Their skin has shriveled on their bones; it has become as dry as a stick.” Verse 9 draws the poem's bleakest conclusion: “Those slain by the sword are better off than those who die of hunger.” And verse 10 states, in the poem's own flat words, the thing the second poem prayed about: “The hands of compassionate women have cooked their own children, who became their food in the destruction of the daughter of my people.” The poem does not linger and does not explain. It says it and moves on, the way the whole book says unbearable things plainly.

Then the poem assigns the cause, and it is not Babylon's strength. Verse 11: “He has kindled a fire in Zion, and it has consumed her foundations.” Verse 12 records the world's disbelief that it could happen at all: “The kings of the earth did not believe, nor any people of the world, that an enemy or a foe could enter the gates of Jerusalem.” Jerusalem's fall was, to everyone watching, an impossible event. Verse 13 explains how the impossible happened, from the inside: “But this was for the sins of her prophets and the guilt of her priests, who shed the blood of the righteous in her midst.” The men charged with speaking for God and guarding the altar had blood on them. By verses 14 and 15 those same men are wandering blind in the streets, defiled, untouchable, with the crowds shouting after them, “Go away! Unclean!” and “Away, away! Do not touch us!” They fled and wandered, and even the nations turned them away. Verse 16 completes their fall: “The presence of the LORD has scattered them; He regards them no more.”

The last movement puts the survivors on the walls, watching. Verse 17: “All the while our eyes were failing as we looked in vain for help. We watched from our towers for a nation that could not save us.” Egypt, the old lover from the first poem, never came. Verse 18 says the streets themselves became traps: “They stalked our every step, so that we could not walk in our streets,” and the refrain of a people counting down: “Our end drew near, our time ran out, for our end had come!” Verse 19: “Those who chased us were swifter than the eagles in the sky,” over the mountains and into ambushes in the wilderness. And verse 20 is the capture the whole nation had believed impossible, the king taken in flight: “The LORD’s anointed, the breath of our life, was captured in their pits.” The poem even quotes their dead confidence back at them: “Under his shadow we will live among the nations.” The shadow was gone.

The poem ends by turning outward, and the turn is startling after all this grief: there is a future tense in it. Verse 21 addresses Edom, the neighbor who rejoiced over the fall and whose judgment Obadiah's whole book announced: “So rejoice and be glad, O Daughter of Edom, you who dwell in the land of Uz. Yet the cup will pass to you as well; you will get drunk and expose yourself.” Then verse 22 speaks the first unqualified comfort in the book, and speaks it to Zion: “O Daughter of Zion, your punishment is complete; He will not prolong your exile. But He will punish your iniquity, O Daughter of Edom; He will expose your sins.” Her exile has an end date written on it by the poem itself. His is coming too. The fourth poem closes with the book's arc bending, just slightly, from punishment toward a limit on punishment. One poem remains, and it is not a description at all. It is the survivors themselves, praying.

title: Restore Us to Yourself
subtitle: Lamentations 5
description: The survivors pray the inventory of their disgrace aloud, and the book ends on an unanswered unless.
paragraphs: The last poem is a prayer, spoken not by the city or the sufferer alone but by the survivors together, in the plural, we. It opens by asking God to do the remembering, since He is the only one whose memory can change anything: “Remember, O LORD, what has happened to us. Look and see our disgrace!” Then comes the inventory, and it is deliberately ordinary, the daily texture of life under occupation. “Our inheritance has been turned over to strangers, our houses to foreigners.” Verse 3: “We have become fatherless orphans; our mothers are widows.” Verse 4: “We must buy the water we drink; our wood comes at a price.” Their own wells and woodlots charge them now. Verse 5: “We are closely pursued; we are weary and find no rest.” Verse 6 reaches back across the whole history for the pattern: “We submitted to Egypt and Assyria to get enough bread.” Generation after generation, the same bargain, bread in exchange for submission.

The prayer is honest about whose fault the inheritance is. Verse 7: “Our fathers sinned and are no more, but we bear their punishment.” Verse 8 describes the world turned upside down: “Slaves rule over us; there is no one to deliver us from their hands.” Verse 9: “We get our bread at the risk of our lives because of the sword in the wilderness,” food gathered the way soldiers forage, under threat. Verse 10 gives the famine a temperature: “Our skin is as hot as an oven with fever from our hunger.” None of this is metaphor hunting for sympathy. It is a community reading its own condition aloud to God, item by item, the way you would read a list of damages to the only official who can act on it.

The middle of the prayer is the hardest to read and the poem does not flinch from it. Verse 11: “Women have been ravished in Zion, virgins in the cities of Judah.” It stands in one line, stated, neither hidden nor dwelt on. Verse 12: “Princes have been hung up by their hands; elders receive no respect.” Verse 13: “Young men toil at millstones; boys stagger under loads of wood.” Verse 14 sums up a civilization by its two silences: “The elders have left the city gate; the young men have stopped their music.” The gate was where justice and business and news happened. The music was where joy happened. Both are empty. A whole society can be measured, the poem suggests, by what no longer gathers and what no longer plays.

Verse 15 turns the inventory inward: “Joy has left our hearts; our dancing has turned to mourning.” Verse 16 is the confession again, the one the third poem taught them to make, now spoken by everyone at once: “The crown has fallen from our head. Woe to us, for we have sinned!” Verses 17 and 18 tie the people's dimming to the mountain's desolation: “Because of this, our hearts are faint; because of these, our eyes grow dim,” and then the reason, standing by itself: “because of Mount Zion, which lies desolate, patrolled by foxes.” Foxes walk the temple mount. That image is the prayer's low point, and the poem places it immediately before its highest line, as if the only way up were straight from there.

The last four verses are an argument built on God's own permanence. Verse 19: “You, O LORD, reign forever; Your throne endures from generation to generation.” Crowns fall; this throne does not. But verse 20 turns the permanence into a question, and it is a daring one: “Why have You forgotten us forever? Why have You forsaken us for so long?” If God reigns forever and they are His, why does His memory of them feel so short? Verse 21 is the request the whole book has been traveling toward, the first time anyone in these poems asks God for restoration outright: “Restore us to Yourself, O LORD, so we may return; renew our days as of old.” Restore us to Yourself first, and the return will follow. The geography is secondary. It is the relationship they are asking for. And then verse 22, the book's last line, spoken as the tail of that request: “unless You have utterly rejected us and remain angry with us beyond measure.” The prayer does not end with the answer. It ends with the unless, hanging in the air, and the book simply stops there, with the survivors still on their knees and heaven not yet heard from. Later generations reading this book aloud would repeat verse 21 after verse 22, so the reading would not close on rejection. The book itself does not do that. It leaves the question where the survivors left it: asked, honestly, to the only throne that endures.
